newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kohl to meet Russian premier as Yeltsin surgery nears.
newsitem.headline: Kohl to meet Russian premier as Yeltsin surgery nears.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl was due to make a brief stopover in Moscow on Saturday for talks with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and to get un update on ailing President Boris Yeltsin's health.
Kohl and Chernomyrdin were scheduled to meet at Moscow's Vnukovo airport while the chancellor's plane refuelled on the way home from Japan after an Asian tour.

Itar-Tass news agency said Kohl, who has closer ties with Yeltsin than any other Western leader and last saw him in September, would discuss the political situation in Russia, economic reforms and Yeltsin's health. It gave no other details.

The health of the 65-year-old president has worried Western leaders who regard him as the guarantor of reforms and stability in Russia. Chernomyrdin is his constitutional stand-in and will assume full powers when doctors operate on Yeltsin's heart.
The Russian surgeons have not announced a date for the multiple bypass operation to improve the supply of blood to Yeltsin's heart.
The Russian daily newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda said it would be on Wednesday but gave no source for its report.
U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who will be a consultant to the Russian doctors, said in Houston on Friday that he expected the surgery to go ahead early next week.
DeBakey, who was due to arrive in Moscow on Sunday, said Yeltsin had been treated for anaemia and thyroid problems but that he appeared now to be ready for surgery.
"On the basis of what they have told me, it looks like we should be able to go ahead with the operation early next week. He's improved," he told Reuters.
DeBakey, 88, said he would meet Yeltsin's medical team on Monday for final consultations.
He examined Yeltsin in late September and predicted a full recovery for the president, but recommended that he rest for at least six weeks before the operation.

DeBakey has posted a special page on the Internet which could be updated during his visit. On Saturday it carried a statement that no information could currently be provided on Yeltsin's state of health.
Chernomyrdin has already taken on some of Yeltsin's duties and, if all goes according to plan, will assume his full powers for only a few hours.
If the president does not recover, the prime minister would take over for three months to prepare for an election.

Chernomyrdin, 58, is widely regarded in the West as a solid, reliable deputy to Yeltsin but Kohl may have been keen to take another look at the man who will briefly have control of Russia's nuclear weapons.
Yeltsin's four-month absence from the Kremlin has prompted talk of a power struggle from which Chernomyrdin has sought to distance himself in public.
The prime minister spent the first part of Saturday at talks with trade union leaders trying to head off a nationwide protest threatened in many branches of industry on Tuesday.

Unpaid wages have also prompted warnings of a virtual collapse in the armed forces. Chernomyrdin spent Friday in the provincial city of Ryazan visiting airborne troops with Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who told journalists the premier was "deeply concerned by the state of affairs in the army".
